claim: The DSM-5 categorizes alcohol as one of the few drugs whose dependence can produce neurocognitive disorders such as alcohol-related dementia.
source: The DSM-5 categorizes alcohol as one of the few drugs whose dependence can produce neurocognitive disorders such as alcohol-related dementia (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to American Psychiatric Association, 2013

claim: Value-based decision-making disruption contributes to poor daily function in alcohol dependence.
source: Value-based decision-making is one such cognitive process, with its disruption contributing to poor daily function, that when combined with the emergence of compulsive control contributes to excessive drug-seeking and relapse (Belin et al., 2013; Everitt and Robbins, 2016; Gremel and Lovinger, 2017; Hogarth et al., 2013; Lüscher et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: OFC circuits play a key role in computations related to decision-making and the evaluation of outcomes.
source: Recently, there has been renewed focus on orbital frontal cortex (OFC) circuits in substance use disorder and related behaviors (Everitt and Robbins, 2016; Lüscher et al., 2020; Moorman, 2018; Schoenbaum et al., 2016; Schoenbaum et al., 2006), as they play a key role in computations related to decision-making and the evaluation of outcomes (Fellows, 2007; Stalnaker et al., 2015; Wallis, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fellows, 2007; Stalnaker et al., 2015; Wallis, 2007

claim: Drug dependence has been widely associated with reduced OFC activity and output.
source: Indeed, drug dependence in general has been widely associated with reduced OFC activity and output (Catafau et al., 1999; Lüscher et al., 2020; Schoenbaum et al., 2016; Schoenbaum et al., 2006; Volkow et al., 1997; Volkow and Fowler, 1994).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: In alcohol-dependent individuals, reduced OFC activity correlates with aberrant value-based decision-making.
source: In alcohol-dependent individuals, reduced OFC activity correlates with aberrant value-based decision-making (Boettiger et al., 2007; Duka et al., 2011; Forbes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boettiger et al., 2007; Duka et al., 2011; Forbes et al., 2014

claim: OFC hyperactivity has been observed in alcohol dependence in response to predictive information.
source: However, OFC hyperactivity has been observed in alcohol dependence in response to predictive information (Hermann et al., 2006; Reinhard et al., 2015; Tapert et al., 2003) and during approach behaviors (Ernst et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hermann et al., 2006; Reinhard et al., 2015; Tapert et al., 2003; Ernst et al., 2014

claim: Rodent and non-human primate models of alcohol dependence have identified long-lasting changes to OFC neuron excitability, structure, and transmission.
source: In concert, both rodent and non-human primate models of alcohol dependence have identified long-lasting changes to OFC neuron excitability, structure, and transmission (Nimitvilai et al., 2017; Nimitvilai et al., 2016; Renteria et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nimitvilai et al., 2017; Nimitvilai et al., 2016; Renteria et al., 2018

claim: OFC excitatory projections synapse onto direct and indirect pathways in the dorsal striatum.
source: One such circuit is OFC excitatory projections into basal ganglia, with synapses onto direct and indirect pathways in the dorsal striatum (DS) (Renteria et al., 2018; Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Renteria et al., 2018; Wall et al., 2013

claim: Inhibition of OFC-DS transmission results in habitual control.
source: Excitatory transmission from OFC-DS projections carries information that may support value-based decision-making, as inhibition of transmission results in habitual control (Gremel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gremel et al., 2016

claim: Chronic alcohol exposure selectively attenuated OFC-DS transmission onto dopamine-type 1 (D1) spiny projection neurons of the direct pathway.
source: We recently found that chronic alcohol exposure selectively attenuated output of this circuit, with a long-lasting reduction in OFC-DS transmission onto dopamine-type 1 (D1) spiny projection neurons (SPNs) of the direct pathway (Renteria et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Renteria et al., 2018

claim: Chronic alcohol exposure produces a loss of value-based decision-making.
source: In addition, chronic alcohol exposure produces a loss of value-based decision-making (Corbit et al., 2012; Dickinson et al., 2002; Renteria et al., 2018) and reductions in associated OFC activity (Catafau et al., 1999; Lüscher et al., 2020; Schoenbaum et al., 2016; Schoenbaum et al., 2006; Volkow et al., 1997; Volkow and Fowler, 1994).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Increasing OFC activity rescued the behavioral phenotype of loss of value-based decision-making following chronic alcohol exposure.
source: Indeed, this behavioral phenotype was rescued by increasing OFC activity (Renteria et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Renteria et al., 2018

claim: Hyperactivity of OFC-DS circuits has been implicated in obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD).
source: However, dependence has also been associated with compulsive phenotypes (Everitt and Robbins, 2016; Everitt and Robbins, 2005; Lüscher et al., 2020), and hyperactivity of OFC-DS circuits has been implicated in obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) (Lüscher et al., 2020; Milad and Rauch, 2012; Pauls et al., 2014; Robbins et al., 2019), as well as animal models of compulsive (Ahmari et al., 2013) and compulsive behaviors (Pascoli et al., 2018; Pascoli et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Increased OFC terminal activity was observed in mice when they self-stimulated ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons, despite the presence of a punishing foot-shock.
source: Indeed, increased OFC terminal activity was observed in mice when they self-stimulated ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons, despite the presence of a punishing foot-shock (Pascoli et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pascoli et al., 2018

claim: Postsynaptic potentiation of OFC-DS transmission corresponds to compulsive self-stimulation behavior.
source: This corresponded to postsynaptic potentiation of OFC-DS transmission (Pascoli et al., 2018), suggesting that increased transmission from OFC into basal ganglia circuits contributes to the emergence of compulsive actions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pascoli et al., 2018 and logical inference

claim: Chronic alcohol exposure selectively enhances OFC-DS activity associated with action while reducing OFC-DS activity during periods associated with outcome retrieval.
source: Here we examine mechanisms underlying how drug dependence affects OFC-DS circuit information representation and its control over decision-making. Using a well-established model of alcohol dependence in mice, we find that chronic alcohol exposure selectively enhances OFC-DS activity associated with action while reducing OFC-DS activity during periods associated with outcome retrieval through downregulation of D1 receptor function in SPNs and enhanced endocannabinoid (eCB) signaling at OFC-D1 SPN synapses in the DS.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Disrupted OFC-DS terminal activity was due to a dysfunction of dopamine-type 1 receptors on spiny projection neurons.
source: Disrupted OFC-DS terminal activity was due to a dysfunction of dopamine-type 1 receptors on spiny projection neurons (D1R SPNs) that resulted in increased retrograde endocannabinoid signaling at OFC-D1R SPN synapses reducing OFC-DS transmission.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Blocking CB1 receptors restored OFC-DS activity in vivo and rescued outcome-based control over decision-making.
source: Blocking CB1 receptors restored OFC-DS activity in vivo and rescued outcome-based control over decision-making.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Mice were exposed to ethanol vapor for 16 hr each day for four consecutive days followed by a 3 day withdrawal, repeated for four consecutive weeks.
source: Performed in three cohort replications, mice (Air n = 10, CIE n = 12) were exposed to ethanol vapor for 16 hr each day for four consecutive days followed by a 3 day withdrawal. This cycle of ethanol vapor and withdrawal was repeated for four consecutive weeks and resulted in blood ethanol concentrations of 33.70 ± 2.24 mM (mean ± SEM) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and methods description

claim: CIE exposure resulted in blood ethanol concentrations of 33.70 ± 2.24 mM.
source: This cycle of ethanol vapor and withdrawal was repeated for four consecutive weeks and resulted in blood ethanol concentrations of 33.70 ± 2.24 mM (mean ± SEM) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurement data

claim: Chronic alcohol exposure did not prevent mice from learning to lever press for food.
source: Chronic alcohol exposure did not prevent mice from learning to lever press for food. Air control mice and CIE-exposed mice made the same number of lever presses (repeated-measures ANOVA: main effect of Training day: F(8, 160)=43.10, p<0.0001; no main effect of CIE exposure or interaction: Fs < 0.16) (Figure 1F)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Air control mice and CIE-exposed mice pressed the lever at roughly equal rates during training.
source: and pressed the lever at roughly equal rates (repeated-measures ANOVA: main effect of Training day: F(8, 160)=27.42, p<0.0001; no main effect of treatment or interaction: Fs < 1.22) (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: CIE mice had shorter intervals between lever presses within a bout compared to Air mice.
source: However, Air and CIE mice differentially executed these bouts, with CIE mice having shorter intervals between lever presses within a bout (inter-press interval, Air: 1.84 s ± 0.05, n = 1514; CIE: 1.31 s ± 0.04, n = 1842; KS test: D = 0.17, p<0.0001) (Figure 1L)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: CIE mice had shorter bout durations compared to Air mice.
source: resulting in shorter bout durations (Air: 19.15 s ± 0.59, n = 1514; CIE: 13.59 s ± 0.41, n = 1842; KS test: D = 0.14, p<0.0001) (Figure 1M).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Chronic alcohol exposure led to a change in action execution, manifested as faster completion of lever press bouts.
source: Thus, chronic alcohol exposure led to a change in action execution, manifested as faster completion of lever press bouts.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing shorter inter-press intervals and bout durations

claim: CIE led to increased OFC-DS Ca2+ activity at the onset of lever press bout when all event trials were collapsed across mice.
source: When all event trials where collapsed across mice, we found increased OFC-DS activity at the onset of lever press bout (false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected two-sided permutation test, all event trials: Air: n = 1363, CIE n = 1650, p<0.05), and net area under the curve (AUC) analyses showed a significant difference between Air and CIE mice (Air: −0.40 ± 0.08, n = 1363; CIE: −0.05 ± 0.06, n = 1650; unpaired t-test: t3011 = 3.70, p<0.001) (Figure 1N).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Air controls showed a large significant increase in OFC-DS terminal activity during the period associated with outcome retrieval following reward delivery.
source: In contrast, when we examined OFC-DS activity during the period associated with outcome retrieval following reward delivery (first head entry after outcome delivery), we found the opposite pattern. There, in both all event and session average analyses, Air controls showed a large significant increase in OFC-DS terminal activity, whereas in CIE mice, this was significantly blunted (FDR-corrected two-sided permutation test, all event trials: Air: n = 521, CIE: n = 682; session average: Air: n = 34; CIE: n = 38) (Figure 1P,Q).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In CIE mice, OFC-DS terminal activity during outcome retrieval was significantly blunted compared to Air controls.
source: There, in both all event and session average analyses, Air controls showed a large significant increase in OFC-DS terminal activity, whereas in CIE mice, this was significantly blunted (FDR-corrected two-sided permutation test, all event trials: Air: n = 521, CIE: n = 682; session average: Air: n = 34; CIE: n = 38) (Figure 1P,Q).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There was an overall decrease in the net AUC in CIE mice compared to Air mice during outcome retrieval.
source: Furthermore, there was an overall decrease in the net AUC in CIE mice compared to Air mice (all event trials: Air: 1.00 ± 0.16, n = 521; CIE: 0.24 ± 0.11, n = 682; unpaired t-test: t1201 = 4.12, p<0.0001; session average: Air: 1.22 ± 0.4, n = 34; CIE: 0.04 ± 0.37, n = 38; unpaired t-test: t70 = 2.18, p<0.05) (Figure 1P,Q).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Air mice reduced responding following outcome devaluation, while CIE mice did less so.
source: Pre-planned comparisons on normalized data to account for differences in response rates between individual mice showed that Air reduced responding following outcome devaluation, while CIE mice did less so (repeated-measures ANOVA: main effect of valuation state: F(1, 10)=6.36, p<0.05; no main effect of CIE exposure or interaction: Fs < 2.98; pre-planned corrected comparisons between Valued and Devalued days: Air p<0.02; CIE p>0.6) (Figure 1U, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Air mice differentially distributed lever pressing between devalued and valued days, and CIE mice did not.
source: Indeed, Air mice differentially distributed lever pressing between devalued and valued days, and CIE mice did not (one-sample paired t-test vs. 0.5; Air-t4 = 3.68, p<0.05; CIE t6 = 0.54, p=0.30).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The reduced calcium activity in OFC-DS terminals is suggestive of a decrease in presynaptic transmission.
source: The reduced calcium activity in OFC-DS terminals is suggestive of a decrease in presynaptic transmission.
evidence: Inferred from the observed calcium activity data

claim: CIE results in a selective and long-lasting decrease in presynaptic OFC transmission onto D1 SPNs of the direct pathway, but not dopamine type-2 (D2) SPNs of the indirect pathway.
source: However, we previously found CIE results in a selective and long-lasting decrease in presynaptic OFC transmission onto D1 SPNs of the direct pathway, but not dopamine type-2 (D2) SPNs of the indirect pathway (Renteria et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Renteria et al., 2018

claim: The reduction in OFC-D1 SPN transmission was stable and persistent across 3 weeks of chronic withdrawal.
source: This reduction in OFC-D1 SPN transmission was stable and persistent across 3 weeks of chronic withdrawal (Renteria et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Renteria et al., 2018

claim: The cell-type-specific decrease in presynaptic transmission may be mediated by a CIE-induced alteration in eCB signaling.
source: As an OFC-DS projection neuron most likely sends collaterals to both D1 SPNs and D2 SPNs (Wall et al., 2013), the cell-type-specific decrease in presynaptic transmission may be mediated by a CIE-induced alteration in eCB signaling (Henderson-Redmond et al., 2016; Parsons and Hurd, 2015; Pava and Woodward, 2012).
evidence: Inferred from prior research and supported by citations

claim: eCBs are produced and released from the postsynaptic cell and act as a retrograde signal to activate presynaptic cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptors, resulting in an inhibition of presynaptic calcium and a subsequent decrease in neurotransmitter release.
source: eCBs are produced and released from the postsynaptic cell and act as a retrograde signal to activate presynaptic cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptors, resulting in an inhibition of presynaptic calcium and a subsequent decrease in neurotransmitter release (Castillo et al., 2012; Gerdeman et al., 2002; Heifets and Castillo, 2009; Kano et al., 2009; Kreitzer and Regehr, 2001; Lovinger, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: CB1 receptors have been implicated in habitual action control.
source: In the dorsal striatum, CB1 receptors have been implicated in habitual action control (Hilário et al., 2007; Nazzaro et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hilário et al., 2007; Nazzaro et al., 2012

claim: Activation of CB1 receptors on OFC terminals in DS has been shown to disrupt sensitivity to changes in expected outcome value.
source: and activation of CB1 receptors on OFC terminals in DS has been shown to disrupt sensitivity to changes in expected outcome value (Gremel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gremel et al., 2016

claim: Bath application of a CB1 receptor agonist (WIN 55,212–2) resulted in a similar decrease in EPSC amplitude between Air and CIE-exposed mice.
source: We applied a CB1 receptor agonist (1 µM WIN 55,212–2) (Figure 2E,F), but found a similar decrease in EPSC amplitude between Air (44.72 ± 1.98% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 6, paired t-test vs. baseline: t5 = 27.96, p<0.0001) and CIE-exposed mice (47.08 ± 9.03% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 6, paired t-test vs. baseline: t5 = 5.86, p<0.01) (unpaired t-test comparing Air and CIE mice: t10 = 0.25, p=0.80).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: A 10 min bath application of DHPG (50 µM) paired with postsynaptic depolarization to 0 mV resulted in LTD of optically evoked EPSCs in both Air and CIE mice.
source: A 10 min bath application of DHPG (50 µM) paired with postsynaptic depolarization to 0 mV, resulted in LTD of optically evoked EPSCs (Air: 54.60 ± 8.40% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 6, paired t-test vs. baseline: t5 = 5.41, p<0.01; CIE: 46.68 ± 4.97% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 5, paired t-test vs. baseline: t4 = 10.74, p<0.001) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: DHPG-induced LTD was of similar magnitude between Air and CIE-exposed mice.
source: However, this DHPG-induced LTD was of similar magnitude between Air and CIE-exposed mice (unpaired t-test: t9 = 0.77, p=0.46) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Bath application of a CB1 receptor antagonist, SR141716 (1 µM) showed the observed LTD to be CB1 receptor dependent in both Air and CIE groups.
source: Bath application of a CB1 receptor antagonist, SR141716 (1 µM) showed the observed LTD to be CB1 receptor dependent in both groups (Air: 103.2 ± 5.85% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 4, paired t-test vs. baseline: t3 = 0.54, p=0.63; CIE: 108.3 ± 5.85% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 6 paired t-test vs. baseline: t5 = 0.96, p=0.38) (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Activation of D1 receptors by bath application of SKF 81297 (3 µM) in Air controls blocked DHPG-LTD.
source: We found that activation of D1 receptors by bath application of SKF 81297 (3 µM) in Air controls blocked DHPG-LTD (96.32 ± 10.41% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 6, paired t-test vs. baseline: t5 = 0.35, p=0.74) but had no effect in CIE-exposed mice (56.12 ± 4.85% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 7, paired t-test vs. baseline: t6 = 9.06, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Activation of D1 receptors had no effect on DHPG-LTD in CIE-exposed mice.
source: We found that activation of D1 receptors by bath application of SKF 81297 (3 µM) in Air controls blocked DHPG-LTD (96.32 ± 10.41% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 6, paired t-test vs. baseline: t5 = 0.35, p=0.74) but had no effect in CIE-exposed mice (56.12 ± 4.85% of baseline at 30–40 min, n = 7, paired t-test vs. baseline: t6 = 9.06, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The LTD that CIE mice continued to express in the presence of D1 agonist was still CB1 receptor dependent.
source: The LTD that CIE mice continued to express was still CB1 receptor dependent, as bath application of SR141716 (1 µM) blocked the DHPG- LTD (104.2 ± 11.55% baseline at 30–40 min, n = 5, paired t-test vs. baseline: t4 = 0.37, p=0.73) (Figure 2K,L).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: D1 receptor activation increases excitability of D1 SPNs.
source: First, D1 receptor activation in vitro has been shown to increase excitability of D1 SPNs (Hernández-López et al., 1997; Planert et al., 2013; Surmeier et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hernández-López et al., 1997; Planert et al., 2013; Surmeier et al., 2007

claim: Washing on D1 agonist, SKF 81297 (10 µM), enhanced D1 SPN action potential firing in response to current injections in the DS of Air controls.
source: Similar to previous findings, we found that washing on D1 agonist, SKF 81297 (10 µM), enhanced D1 SPN action potential firing in response to current injections in the DS of Air controls (repeated-measures ANOVA: interaction (Current × SKF 81297): F(10, 90)=5.72, p<0.0001; main effect of Current: F(10, 90)=22.46, p<0.0001; main effect of SKF 81297: F(1, 9)=32.37, p=0.0003) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Bath application of SKF 81297 had no effect on D1 SPN excitability in CIE mice.
source: In contrast, bath application of SKF 81297 had no effect on D1 SPN excitability in CIE mice (repeated-measures ANOVA: no interaction [Current × SKF 81297]: F(10, 80)=0.28, p=0.98; main effect of Current: F(10, 80)=29.87, p<0.0001, but no main effect of SKF 81297: F(1, 8)=0.09, p=0.77) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: D1 receptor signaling is disrupted in CIE mice.
source: This suggests that D1 receptor signaling is disrupted in CIE mice and is in line with our previous data in which a D1 agonist failed to modulate DHPG-LTD in CIE mice (Figure 2K,L).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing lack of D1 agonist effects in CIE mice

claim: An imbalance in striatal dopamine induced rotational behavior.
source: To test whether CIE alters the function of DS D1 receptors in vivo, we relied on previous findings where an imbalance in striatal dopamine induced rotational behavior (Glick et al., 1976; Martín et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glick et al., 1976; Martín et al., 2008

claim: Air mice showed the predicted increase in CW rotations following unilateral D1 agonist injection, while CIE mice showed reduced D1-agonist induced rotational behavior.
source: While Air mice showed the predicted increase in CW rotations, CIE mice showed reduced D1-agonist induced rotational behavior. A one-way ANOVA (F(3, 24)=9.31, p<0.001) showed that Air controls had significantly more CW rotations than CCW rotations (Bonferroni corrected, p<0.001) and had more CW rotations compared to CIE mice (Bonferroni corrected, p<0.05) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There was no difference in the total number of rotations between Air and CIE mice.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in the total number of rotations between Air and CIE mice (Air: 62.13 ± 4.54, n = 8; CIE: 57.67 ± 7.76, n = 6; unpaired t-test: t12 = 0.53, p=0.61) (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The percentage of CW rotations out of total rotations in CIE mice was significantly lower compared to Air controls.
source: However, the percentage of CW rotations out of total rotations in CIE mice was significantly lower compared to Air controls (Air: 73.72 ± 4.08, n = 8; CIE: 47.72 ± 4.21, n = 6; unpaired t-test: t12 = 4.36, p<0.001) (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Western blot analysis showed no change in D1 receptor expression in the DS between CIE and Air mice.
source: The blunted D1 receptor agonist response in CIE mice could be due to alterations in D1 receptor expression; however, Western blot analysis showed no change in D1 receptor expression in the DS between CIE and Air mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis

claim: CIE results in disruption of D1 receptor function downstream of D1 receptor activation.
source: Together, these data provide evidence that CIE results in disruption of D1 receptor function downstream of D1 receptor activation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing D1 receptor dysfunction

claim: Depolarization to +50 mV for 10 s resulted in a short-term decrease of EPSC amplitudes in both Air and CIE mice that was CB1 receptor dependent.
source: To induce DSE of optically evoked EPSCs from OFC terminals (Figure 4A), D1 SPNs were depolarized to +50 mV for 10 s which resulted in a short-term decrease of EPSC amplitudes in both Air (DSE Air: 25.78 ± 3.82, n = 8, three mice, paired t-test vs. baseline: t7 = 6.75, p<0.001) and CIE mice (DSE CIE: 42.10 ± 8.25, n = 9, three mice, paired t-test vs. baseline: t8 = 15.31, p<0.0001) that was CB1 receptor dependent (bath application of SR141716 [1 µM], DSE Air: 2.71 ± 3.09, n = 5, paired t-test vs. baseline: t4 = 0.88, p=0.43; DSE CIE: 1.77 ± 5.20, n = 6, paired t-test vs. baseline: t5 = 0.34, p=0.75) (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: CIE mice showed a larger magnitude of DSE than did Air controls.
source: We found that CIE mice showed a larger magnitude of DSE than did Air controls (unpaired t-test Air vs. CIE: t15 = 3.53, p<0.01), indicating a CIE-induced increase in eCB signaling in OFC-D1 SPN transmission (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Air and CIE mice showed a similar magnitude of DSE when EPSCs were electrically evoked.
source: In contrast to optically evoked EPSCs at OFC-D1 SPNs synapses (Figure 4A–C), Air and CIE mice showed a similar magnitude of DSE when EPSCs were electrically evoked (unpaired t-test Air vs. CIE: t10 = 0.52, p=0.61) (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The CIE-induced increase in DSE was cell-type selective as no difference in DSE of D2 SPNs of Air and CIE mice was observed with either optical stimulation of OFC terminals or local electrical stimulation.
source: Furthermore, the CIE-induced increase in DSE was cell-type selective as we observed no difference in DSE of D2 SPNs of Air and CIE mice with either optical stimulation of OFC terminals or local electrical stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The increase in DSE of OFC transmission onto D1 SPNs following chronic alcohol exposure is at least partially selective to the OFC input.
source: These results suggest that the increase in DSE of OFC transmission onto D1 SPNs following chronic alcohol exposure is at least partially selective to the OFC input.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of optical and electrical stimulation results

claim: Systemic administration of SR141716 had no obvious effect on gross lever press-related behavior.
source: Similar to prior findings that blocking CB1 receptors does not interfere with the ability to lever press (Hilário et al., 2007), we also found that systemic administration of SR141716 had no obvious effect on gross lever press-related behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Hilário et al., 2007

claim: Systemic injection of CB1 receptor antagonist decreased OFC terminal activity in DS during initiation of lever press bouts in both Air and CIE mice.
source: Systemic injection of CB1 receptor antagonist was found to decrease OFC terminal activity in DS during initiation of lever press bouts in both Air and CIE mice (Figure 5), suggesting the effect the antagonist exerted was not through activation of CB1 receptors on OFC terminals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Blocking CB1 receptors had little effect on OFC-DS transmission during outcome retrieval epochs in Air controls but significantly increased activity in CIE mice.
source: In contrast, blocking CB1 receptors had little effect on OFC-DS transmission during outcome retrieval epochs in Air controls but significantly increased activity in CIE mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Systemic administration of the CB1 antagonist in CIE mice produced a significant and sustained increase in OFC terminal activity during the period of outcome retrieval.
source: In contrast, systemic administration of the CB1 antagonist in CIE mice produced a significant and sustained increase in OFC terminal activity during this period of outcome retrieval (FDR-corrected two-sided permutation test, all event trials: Vehicle: n = 275; SR141716: n = 219; session average: Vehicle: n = 10; SR141716: n = 10) (Figure 5N,P).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Locally blocking CB1 receptors in the DS of CIE mice was sufficient to restore value-based decision-making.
source: Thus, locally blocking CB1 receptors in the DS of CIE mice was sufficient to restore value-based decision-making.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing restored outcome devaluation sensitivity

claim: CIE mice that were given an injection of SR141716 in the DS significantly decreased lever press responding on the devalued day relative to the value day.
source: However, CIE mice that were given an injection of SR141716 in the DS significantly decreased lever press responding on the devalued day relative to the value day (Figure 6F). A repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant interaction (Training day × Treatment: F(3, 28)=4.41, p=0.01) and main effect of Devaluation day (F(1, 28)=33.28, p<0.0001) but no main effect of Treatment (F < 0.1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: CIE induces long-lasting, computational-specific changes to cortical transmission in part through cell-type, synapse-specific changes in postsynaptic modulation of cortical terminal release.
source: Thus, CIE induces long-lasting, computational-specific changes to cortical transmission in part through cell-type, synapse-specific changes in postsynaptic modulation of this cortical terminal release.
evidence: Inferred from the totality of experimental findings

claim: The loss of D1 receptor function in SPNs of CIE exposed mice may be directly related to the enhancement of eCB signaling.
source: The loss of D1 receptor function in SPNs of CIE exposed mice may be directly related to the enhancement of eCB signaling (Figures 4 and 7).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by figure references

claim: D1 receptor activation may reduce anandamide (AEA) signaling.
source: Previous works have shown dopamine and eCB signaling interact in which D1 receptor activation may reduce anandamide (AEA) signaling (André et al., 2010; Patel et al., 2003) (but see Giuffrida et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to André et al., 2010; Patel et al., 2003

claim: DSE has widely been shown to be mediated by 2-arachidonoyl glycerol (2-AG).
source: However, DSE has widely been shown to be mediated by 2-arachidonoyl glycerol (2-AG), and a CIE-induced increase in 2-AG may contribute to the present effects.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about DSE mechanisms

claim: An inhibitor of 2-AG, DO34, was found to reduce habitual responding in alcohol seeking.
source: Others have shown that habitual alcohol seeking may be mediated by an increase in 2-AG, as an inhibitor, DO34, was found to reduce habitual responding (Gianessi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gianessi et al., 2020

claim: eCBs can reduce dopamine release in nucleus accumbens through reducing cortical drive.
source: For example, as eCBs can reduce dopamine release in nucleus accumbens through reducing cortical drive (Mateo et al., 2017), there may also be a CIE-induced decrease in endogenous D1R activation at OFC-D1 SPN synapses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mateo et al., 2017

claim: The synapse and cell-type-specific alterations in orbitostriatal transmission are likely the result of ethanol-induced changes in many neuromodulatory and synaptic signaling systems.
source: Given the large number of synaptic and molecular targets that chronic ethanol exposure can modulate (Abrahao et al., 2017; Lovinger and Roberto, 2013; Roberto and Varodayan, 2017), the synapse and cell-type-specific alterations in orbitostriatal transmission that we have observed are likely the result of ethanol-induced changes in many neuromodulatory and synaptic signaling systems.
evidence: Inferred from prior research and supported by citations

claim: The CIE-induced alterations in eCB-mediated signaling and plasticity were found to be at least, in part, specific to the OFC input.
source: The CIE-induced alterations in eCB-mediated signaling and plasticity presented here were found to be at least, in part, specific to the OFC input.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of optical and electrical stimulation results

claim: Enhanced eCB signaling is not expected to apply to thalamostriatal inputs to D1 SPNs, as they lack CB1 receptors at presynaptic terminals.
source: However, enhanced eCB signaling is not expected to apply to thalamostriatal inputs to D1 SPNs, as they lack CB1 receptors at presynaptic terminals (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2015

claim: Differences in instrumental responding and outcome encoding may result from differentially engaged local regulation of OFC-DS transmission.
source: These observations suggest that differences in instrumental responding and outcome encoding may result from differentially engaged local regulation of OFC-DS transmission.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of differential CB1 antagonist effects

claim: OFC may pass into striatum information pertaining to more than one type of computation employed during outcome devaluation.
source: As prior work showed a dependency of outcome devaluation on the activity of OFC-DS terminals (Gremel et al., 2016), it is important to note that our current findings suggest that OFC may pass into striatum information pertaining to more than one type of computation employed during outcome devaluation.
evidence: Inferred from current findings and supported by citation to Gremel et al., 2016

claim: Chronic heavy alcohol consumption increases excitatory drive and decreases local inhibition within the putamen or dorsolateral striatum (DLS).
source: Work performed in non-human primates suggests chronic heavy alcohol consumption increases excitatory drive and decreases local inhibition within the putamen or dorsolateral striatum (DLS), an area supporting habitual action control (Cuzon Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cuzon Carlson et al., 2011

claim: Alcohol exposure may result in a decreased ability of associative cortical input to control DS output as well as disinhibition of DLS.
source: Thus, it may be that alcohol exposure results in a decreased ability of associative cortical input to control DS output as well as disinhibition of DLS.
evidence: Speculative inference based on prior research findings

claim: Mice were housed in groups of 2–4, with mouse chow and water ad libitum and were kept on a 14 hr light/10 hr dark cycle.
source: Adult (>8 weeks) male and female mice were housed in groups of 2–4, with mouse chow (Purina 5015) and water ad libitum and were kept on a 14 hr light/10 hr dark cycle.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: Mice were exposed to four rounds of ethanol vapor or air and repeated withdrawal, with each round consisting of 16 hr of vapor exposure followed by an 8 hr withdrawal, repeated for four consecutive days.
source: Mice were exposed to four rounds of ethanol vapor or air and repeated withdrawal (Becker, 1994; Becker and Lopez, 2004; Griffin et al., 2009; Lopez and Becker, 2005). Each round consisted of 16 hr of vapor exposure followed by an 8 hr withdrawal, repeated for four consecutive days.
evidence: Describes experimental methods and supported by citations

claim: Blood ethanol concentrations were collected at the end of each round from sentinel mice with a mean BEC of 34.7 ± 2.0 mM.
source: Blood ethanol concentrations (BEC) were collected at the end of each round from sentinel mice (mean BEC = 34.7 ± 2.0 mM).
evidence: Describes experimental measurement data

claim: Two days prior to training, mice were food restricted and maintained at ~ 90% of their baseline body weight throughout training and testing.
source: Two days prior to training, mice were food restricted and maintained at ~ 90% of their baseline body weight throughout training and testing.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: Mice were trained to press a single lever for a food reinforcer under various schedules of reinforcement.
source: Mice were placed in sound attenuating operant boxes (Med-Associates) and were trained to press a single lever (left or right) for a food reinforcer (chow pellet). Mice were first trained to retrieve the outcome, in the absence of levers, under a random time schedule (RT60) in which the outcome was delivered on average every 60 s. Mice were then trained on a continuous reinforcement schedule (CRF) in each context in which each lever press produced a single outcome, and the maximum number of reinforcers earned in three daily sessions being 5, 15, and 30, respectively. Following CRF training, mice were trained under a random ratio (RR) schedule of reinforcement. Mice received two days of training in RR10 (on average the 10th lever press produces the outcome), followed by 4 days under RR20.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: Devaluation testing through sensory-specific satiation was conducted across 2 days: a valued day and a devalued day.
source: Devaluation testing through sensory-specific satiation was conducted across 2 days: a valued day and a devalued day. Mice were allowed to prefeed ad libitum for 1 hr on the food pellet outcome previously earned by lever pressing (devalued day) or a 20% sucrose solution to control for satiety (valued day). Each day immediately following prefeeding, mice underwent a 5 min extinction test in which the number of lever presses made were recorded, but no outcome was delivered.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: Fluorescence emissions were collected with a bifurcated fiber which allowed for simultaneous recording of two mice.
source: Fluorescence emissions were collected with a bifurcated fiber (Thorlabs), which allowed for simultaneous recording of two mice.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: Only sessions in which the 97.5% of ∆F/F0 across the entire session trace exceeded a 1% change from baseline fluorescence were included.
source: Only sessions in which the 97.5% of ∆F/F0, across the entire session trace (independent of any behavioral response), exceeded a 1% change from baseline fluorescence were included (Markowitz et al., 2018).
evidence: Describes data inclusion criteria and supported by citation

source: Coronal slices (250 μm thick) containing the DS were prepared using a Pelco easiSlicer (Ted Pella Inc, Redding, CA).

source: Picrotoxin (50 µM) was included in the recording ACSF to block GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic currents.

source: For long-term depression (LTD) experiments, EPSCs were evoked at 0.05 Hz for a 10 min baseline, followed by a 10 min bath application of (S)−3,5-dihydroxy-phenylglycine (S-DHPG) (50 µM) paired with depolarization to 0 mV.

source: For depolarization-induced suppression of excitation (DSE), EPSCs were evoked at a rate of 0.2 Hz for a 30 s baseline followed by a 10 s depolarization to +50 mV.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

source: Tissue punches from the medial DS were prepared using a disposable biopsy puncher (Integra, #3331-A) from fresh-frozen brains of CIE or air-exposed mice and kept at −80°C until further processing.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

source: For rotation behaviors, mice received a unilateral injection (left hemisphere) of 300 nL of SKF81297 (13.49 mM) at a rate of 100 nL/min 20 min prior to testing.
evidence: Describes experimental methods

claim: For CB1 receptor antagonist effects on devaluation, 300 nL of an 8 µM solution of SR141716A made up of 75% DMSO and 25% saline was injected into each hemisphere 30 min prior to prefeeding.
source: For CB1 receptor antagonist effects on devaluation, 300 nL of an 8 µM solution of SR141716A made up of 75% DMSO and 25% saline was injected into each hemisphere 30 min prior to prefeeding for outcome devaluation testing.

claim: Statistical significance was defined as an alpha of p≤0.05.
source: Statistical significance was defined as an alpha of p≤0.05.

claim: To determine whether there were significant differences in photometry data between groups, permutation testing was performed.
source: To determine whether there were significant differences in photometry data between groups, permutation testing was performed (Jean-Richard-Dit-Bressel et al., 2020; Pascoli et al., 2018) in which trials of event-related activity from each treatment group were combined and randomly partitioned 1000 times to compute Z-score means and standard deviations across 50 ms bins.
evidence: Describes statistical methods and supported by citations

source: To account for the potential false-discovery rate associated with doing a high number of tests, we applied the Benjamini and Hochberg false discovery rate correction (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
evidence: Describes statistical methods and supported by citation
